paras: The lynching of Sam Gaines was the killing of a Black man by a party of masked men at his cabin ten miles north of Springfield, Robertson County, Tennessee, near the Kentucky line, on the night of March 1, 1881. Gaines was called from his bed and shot to death in front of his wife and children, and no one was reported arrested. Tennessee papers presented the killing as the latest in a run of mob violence in Robertson County, while Kentucky papers repeated a charge that he had been banished for arson.

According to the Springfield special to the Nashville American, Gaines had a reputation as a peaceable man, and the only altercation anyone knew of had occurred in Kentucky a year earlier, when he was said to have choked a white man nearly to death. A separate Nashville dispatch to the Chicago Tribune, which called him "Dennis Galnes" and placed him on the farm of W. F. Putterson, said instead that he had been suspected of arson, ordered to leave the county, and had returned after a stay in Kentucky. The Hartford Herald gave the same account, saying he had been "driven off last fall" over incendiary fires he was charged with and ordered not to return.

Late at night a party of masked men knocked at Gaines's cabin door and asked whether he was asleep. When he opened the door in his night clothes, two of the men seized him and dragged him about fifty yards from the house, where he was shot down in the presence of his wife and children. The guns were held so close that his shirt caught fire, and the body showed five pistol bullets and forty-two duckshot. His body was found the next morning, "full of bullet-holes."

At the coroner's inquest every witness testified that Gaines had a fair character, and the Morristown Gazette reported that his neighbors declared him on oath a "peaceable, good citizen." The killers were supposed to have come from Kentucky, but the Clarksville Chronicle reported that no clue to them had been found. No report of arrests, an indictment or a trial appears in the coverage.

The story spread from the American's Springfield special, which the Memphis Appeal printed in full on March 3 under the line that Gaines was "the ninth man mobbed in Robertson county within the past six months." The special mocked Robertson County as "the champion mob county of the State," and the Appeal's headline scored "Another Mob Murder for Robertson County." The Chicago Tribune likewise placed the killing in the county where the Laprade murder and the lynching of his killers had occurred.

Within Tennessee, the Clarksville Chronicle called it a "most outrageous and brutal murder," and the Morristown Gazette dared the Springfield Record's editor to turn his "corps of lynchers" on Gaines's killers as had been done in the Laprade case. Across the line in Kentucky, the Hartford Herald treated the killing as the "result" of his disobeying an order to stay away, and the Breckenridge News joked that the dead man was not the Kentucky newspaperman of the same name while calling the killers "regulators" and repeating the arson charge.

Shortened wire versions appeared the same day in the New York Sun and New-York Tribune under the heading "A Negro Murdered by Masked Men," and the long special ran in the Alexandria Gazette and the Bristol News. Later briefs in distant papers garbled details, placing the killing at "Springfield, O." or in Montgomery County, while a Minnesota weekly said Gaines "was lynched in Tennessee in a horrible manner without known cause."

The papers disagreed on motive: the Springfield special said no cause was known and surmised revenge by friends of the man he had fought in Kentucky, while the Chicago Tribune and the Hartford Herald attributed the killing to his return after banishment on an arson charge. The Springfield account drew on coroner's-jury testimony that he had no recent difficulty, which the other versions do not address. Accounts also differed on the night of the attack, on the victim's first name, and on the number of attackers, which the Weekly Chillicothe Crisis gave as two.

reader.title: Lynching of Sam Gaines
bases: A party of masked men called Gaines from his house at night and shot him to death, which the papers described as a mob killing (A1, A2, A16).

A masked 'party' with several guns (five pistol bullets plus shot) killed Gaines without any legal process (A1, A3); papers attributed it either to revenge for an old altercation with a white man or to his return after being banished on an arson charge, and a Kentucky paper called the killers 'regulators' (A1, A3, A12, A13).

The Springfield special (A1, A2), a separate Chicago Tribune Nashville special (A3), the Clarksville Chronicle (A8) and two Kentucky weeklies (A12, A13) agree that masked men called Gaines out at night and shot him dead, though they differ on name, place and motive.

accounts.label: Springfield special to the Nashville American
accounts.gist: Masked men called the peaceable Gaines out of bed, dragged him fifty yards and shot him before his family; no cause was known, though the only altercation he had been in was the choking of a white man in Kentucky a year before, so the killers were thought to be from Kentucky.

accounts.label: Chicago Tribune Nashville special
accounts.gist: Unknown persons fired a volley at 'Dennis Galnes' at his door; he had been suspected of arson, ordered to leave the county, and had come back from Kentucky, angering those who had ordered him away.

accounts.label: Kentucky weeklies
accounts.gist: The Hartford Herald said he had been driven off for incendiarism he was charged with and killed for disobeying the order not to return; the Breckenridge News said 'regulators' killed him and that he had set fires.

framing.detail: The Springfield special called the attackers 'ruffians' and Robertson County 'the champion mob county of the State', and the Memphis Appeal headlined it 'Another Mob Murder for Robertson County, the Ninth within a Twelvemonth'.
The Clarksville Chronicle called it a 'most outrageous and brutal murder' by 'dastardly murderers', and the Morristown Gazette called it a 'foul murder'.

The Hartford Herald presented the killing as the 'result' of his disobeying a banishment order over arson, and the Breckenridge News joked that the victim was not the Kentucky newspaperman of the same name while repeating the arson charge.
Northern and Virginia papers ran the American special or its short version under headings such as 'A Negro Murdered by Masked Men'; one Minnesota brief said he 'was lynched'.

versions.value: No cause known; perhaps friends of a person (a white man he choked) he had a difficulty with in Kentucky a year earlier
Suspected or charged with arson, banished, and killed for returning

conflicts.note: The Springfield special, which reports coroner's-jury testimony that he had a fair character and no recent difficulty, is closest to the inquest; the arson version comes from a separate Nashville special and two Kentucky papers across the line.
Only the Chicago Tribune uses 'Dennis'; 'Galnes' may be an OCR or telegraphic variant.
The local Springfield special places it in Robertson County; the Ohio placement is a clear error.
The Springfield special was datelined March 2 and said 'last night'.

versions.value: A party of masked men, two of whom seized him

conflicts.note: The Springfield special's five pistol bullets 'from as many pistols' and shotgun charge suggest more than two.
